newsitem.title: USA: Earplugs accepted as evidence in Oklahoma trial.
newsitem.headline: Earplugs accepted as evidence in Oklahoma trial.

text.p: The judge at the Oklahoma City bombing trial admitted into evidence on Monday earplugs that accused bomber Timothy McVeigh had in his pocket when he was arrested on the day of the blast.
Defence lawyers earlier attacked methods used by the FBI to collect debris from the bomb site in an attempt to show that evidence implicating McVeigh could have been contaminated.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch accepted the earplugs as evidence after the jailer at the Noble County Jail in Perry, Oklahoma, testified that McVeigh had the plugs with him when he was arrested for a traffic violation 90 minutes after the blast.

The prosecution maintains McVeigh, a decorated Gulf War veteran with fierce anti-government views, used the plugs to shield his ears after the April 19, 1995, explosion at the Alfred P. Murrah building that killed 168 people.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy charges. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

The plugs featured prominently in prosecutor Joseph Hartzler's opening statement at the trial last month when he said: "McVeigh liked to consider himself a patriot, someone who could start the second American Revolution.
"Our forefathers ... didn't plant bombs and run away wearing earplugs," Hartzler added.

Matsch had declined to accept the earplugs as evidence last Thursday because he said the prosecution had not established the "chain of custody" of the plugs. Jailer Marcia Moritz established that by stating she received the plugs from McVeigh, although she could not remember the colour of the plugs.

Vivian Dewyse, a chemist at chemical firm ICI, testified about the composition of bomb-grade ammonium nitrate made at the company's plant in Joplin, Missouri, saying it could be distinguished from that of any other North American manufacturer.

The ammonium nitrate used in the bombing was allegedly bought at a farm cooperative in McPherson, Kansas, which sold the ICI brand. The Rocky Mountain News reported on Sunday that prosecutors believed the main component of the Oklahoma City bomb was a version of ammonium nitrate specifically made for bombs, not fertiliser.
The defence had earlier launched a spirited attack on FBI collection-gathering methods at the bomb site.

In most cases, debris considered to be evidence was photographed where it lay before being picked up, Ronald Kelly, a chemist at the Federal Bureau of Investigation's crime laboratory in Washington D.C., testified.

Defence attorney Christopher Tritico got Kelly to concede that an item of evidence was picked up and replaced where it was found before being photographed. Several other items were removed from where they were found and put in plastic bags before being photographed, Kelly said.
The debris appeared to come from the Ryder rental truck that the government says McVeigh used to bomb the federal building.

News reports say some of the debris carried traces of explosives, proving the truck carried the bomb, although that has not yet come out in court. The defence is trying to show the evidence could have been contaminated or tampered with.

A Department of Justice report issued last month sharply criticised the role of several FBI lab employees in the Oklahoma City bombing case and forensic analysis done there is expected to be a controversial area of the government's case against McVeigh.

Kelly, one of several employees from the FBI lab who helped collect evidence after the bombing, said he did not wear any protective clothing except for a freshly-washed set of clothes but he said he did take steps to avoid contamination of evidence.

Tritico sharply questioned Kelly over another piece of the Ryder truck he picked up at a parking lot near the Murrah building. "You received it from a citizen and didn't find it in the parking lot yourself?," he said.
